transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-29 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~38 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Alicia (Firebreak CTO), Tom (Eng), Ravi (Product), Li (SRE)

Auto-generated Summary (brief):
- Intro + quick hosted API demo focusing on streaming behavior, parameter tuning (temp/top_p/max_tokens), and retry/backoff patterns.
- Console tour for cost/latency per-route and Optimize suggestions mentioned.
- Agreed next steps: trial keys, benchmark, POC planning.

Topics: streaming reconnects, partial-chunk semantics, idempotency tokens, console traces, KV cache, batching and cost trade-offs, SOC2/KMS questions.

Action items (recorded): Maya to share trial keys and security pack; Jonah to run a micro-benchmark; Alicia to confirm stakeholders.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, um this is Maya from Redwood Inference, i'll kick us off, quick agenda: demo of hosted chat/textgen streaming basics, show console traces, and then talk about retries and a simple resilience pattern.
[00:18] Alicia: thanks, hey Maya, we just wanna make sure rough alignment on latency — our product needs under 700ms token latency for the live agent flow — and we also have strict audit logs reqs.
[00:30] Maya: got it, that helps, we'll show how streaming chunks look and how you can trace tokens in the console; also we'll touch on audit logs and KMS, soz that will be at the end.
[00:42] Jonah: quick intro from me — i'm Jonah on the SE side, i'll dive into param effects and demo a small reconnect + retry scenario. heads-up transcription may mangle some acronyms.
[00:55] Tom: hi, Tom from Eng — we use websockets today, can you show both streaming over websocket and streaming via http2?
[01:05] Maya: sure — Redwood supports server-sent streaming over the REST endpoints, and websockets can be built on top, but our SDKs handle chunk assembly; we'll show the raw event chunks too.
[01:22] Priya: i'll share my screen to a sandbox, so you can see the streaming payloads and the console trace, okay?
[01:30] Speaker 1: (screen share starts)
[01:34] Priya: alright, sandbox session loaded, first request is a chat generate with temp=0.2 top_p=0.9, max_tokens=150; note we enable early streaming so you see partial tokens every 200ms-ish in this client.
[01:50] Ravi: quick q — when you say partial tokens, are they deterministic or can reconnections produce duplicates?
[02:00] Jonah: good question — partial chunks are incremental deltas; if the client reconnects mid-stream we include a resume token and the model resumes from cache, so duplicates should be minimal. auf, sometimes clients need to dedupe by stream-id.
[02:18] Li: resume token? is that the same as an idempotency key?
[02:25] Jonah: slightly different — idempotency key is for the whole request (prevents duplicate generation on retries), resume token is a per-stream offset so client can pick up a stream without re-gen-ing from scratch. both supported. some SDKs handle it for you.
[02:45] Alicia: and how does that interact with our SSO setup? we need single-sign for console access and audit trails.
[02:52] Maya: we integrate with SAML SSO and support role-based access; console audit events are stored and can be forwarded to your SIEM — we'll attach SOC 2 docs.
[03:08] Priya: ok demo continues: here's a typical 1-turn chat, you can see 3 event chunks: initial meta, token-stream, final completion with usage counts. the console's trace view shows per-token latency and the kernel selection for that run (shows quantized RTX path in this case).
[03:32] Tom: the kernel selection name was mangled in the UI — says QNTZ-RXT-xyz, what does that mean?
[03:38] Jonah: that's a shorthand: QNTZ means quantized, RXT is our internal runtime for certain GPUs — apologies the UI uses internal codes; we'll map them to plain names in the docs we send.
[03:50] [00:04] (small crosstalk)
[04:00] Jonah: now on parameters: temperature affects randomness — we recommend 0.0-0.3 for deterministic assistants, 0.7+ for creative tasks. top_p is an alternate control; using both together is fine but top_p dominates sampling tail.
[04:22] Ravi: any rule-of-thumb for token budget vs latency? we expect variable user messages 20-250 tokens.
[04:30] Jonah: yes — bigger max_tokens only matters for output cap; latency is proportional to generated tokens per step plus overhead. continuous batching can increase throughput but may add a few ms per token; Optimize suggests a batching window for your qps.
[04:50] Priya: here's a small failover test: i'll kill the worker node that's handling the request to simulate a transient capacity issue. you should see a graceful fallback to a compatible model variant.
[05:05] [05:06] (pause, audible UI refresh)
[05:12] Alicia: i see a 503 then a resume? the client got a short reconnect and continued.
[05:18] Jonah: exactly — our smart routing will fallback to a pinned-compatible family if your primary pool is out; the client sees a short retry with exponential backoff. by default we use 3 retries with jitter; you can tune that.
[05:36] Tom: can we change retry counts per-route, per-customer?
[05:40] Maya: yep — routing and retry policies can be set per-route; for Dedicated contracts we embed SLAs and also can set stricter retry windows.
[05:52] Ravi: curious about cost — if fallback goes to a larger model, are we billed at the fallback model's rate?
[05:59] Maya: yes, billing follows the model actually used for inference; the console will show token cost breakdown per-model and per-request. Optimize can propose a quantized variant to match quality.
[06:15] Li: we have to be GDPR-compliant for EU users and need data residency — can hosted API restrict region?
[06:22] Maya: hosted tenants can pin region or we can provision a private deployment in a customer VPC for strict residency. we'll include region options in the proposal.
[06:33] Jonah: back to resilience: a best-practice is to use idempotency keys on client retries, set low initial timeout for streaming receive and exponential backoff for reconnect. we also recommend persistent KV cache for context window reuse — that reduces both latency and cost.
[06:52] Ravi: KV cache for prompt prefixes — how is that instrumented? do we get cache hit metrics?
[06:59] Priya: yes, the runtime reports cache hit/miss rates in the console; Optimize will flag low hit rates and recommend batching or refactor prompts.
[07:12] Tom: about batching — we use bursty traffic. will batching increase tail latency?
[07:18] Jonah: small batching windows reduce cost but can add 10-40ms depending on qps patterns. for your worst-case low-latency paths we recommend a fast-path route with aggressive pinning and minimal batching.
[07:35] [07:36] (short silence)
[07:40] Alicia: show us an idempotency example in the API body? the sample in the docs looked terse.
[07:46] Priya: sure — sending idempotency_key: "firebreak-req-123" in header, and resume_token if resuming. here's a POST payload snippet...
[07:58] (screen scroll)
[08:02] Jonah: note: if you set max_tokens smaller and then resume, we still honor the original seed; set deterministic seeding when you need perfect repeatability.
[08:12] Ravi: are seeds exposed to customers? any security concerns?
[08:17] Maya: seeds are internal metadata used for deterministic runs; we do not surface them as plaintext in logs — audit logs contain run identifiers but not seed values. KMS integration encrypts keys at rest.
[08:33] Li: can we configure log retention to our own S3?
[08:36] Maya: yes, for enterprise we can forward audit logs to your S3 or SIEM. we'll include the retention options and costs.
[08:48] Tom: do you support server-side timeouts we can enforce? like cut-off at 500ms per token to avoid tail-long responses?
[08:56] Jonah: you can set per-route soft and hard timeouts; soft timeout sends a signal to the model to wrap up, hard timeout aborts. also the streaming client receives a final partial.
[09:12] Alicia: let's talk about Console — can you show the per-route cost metrics?
[09:18] Priya: switching to console, here's the route view: token counts, cost per token, latency percentiles, and Optimize recommendations. you can filter by model family and timeframe.
[09:35] Ravi: that Optimize recommendation said 'consider 4-bit quantization' — is that quality-lossy?
[09:41] Jonah: 4-bit quant can introduce slight degradation, depends on task. Optimize runs a small eval suite against your prompt set and shows expected delta; you can set a quality threshold.
[09:55] Maya: quick note on privacy — for hosted, we do ephemeral context caching and can disable retention if needed. Private deployments keep data local.
[10:06] Li: one more thing: we run offline batch reranks for search, can we use embeddings + generative rerank?
[10:13] Jonah: yes, Redwood supports embeddings and cross-embedding rerank pipelines; batching and offline jobs are billed differently. we can share an architecture diagram.
[10:24] [10:25] (background noise)
[10:30] Tom: any pitfalls you typically see on first integration?
[10:33] Maya: common: not using idempotency keys, not deduping partial chunks on reconnect, and aggressive timeouts causing truncated completions; we give a runbook for that.
[10:45] Alicia: ok timeline wise, we want a POC within two weeks if possible. budget review is tuesday.
[10:52] Maya: great — we'll target a POC kickoff asap; i'll send trial keys and a quickstart node/python snippet.
[11:00] Jonah: i'll also prep a micro-benchmark harness that hits your sample messages and returns p50/p95 token latency and cost per 1k tokens.
[11:08] Priya: and i'll attach the console screenshots and a short video of the streaming resume.
[11:14] Ravi: thanks, that helps. any carrier of competitors or lock-in risk? Alicia: our procurement will ask.
[11:21] Maya: we try to be transparent — we'll provide exportable logs and a migration playbook; also provide options for private deployment later.
[11:30] [11:31] (wrap)
[11:34] Maya: recap: next steps per action items, send security docs, trial tokens, micro-benchmark, and schedule POC kickoff. thanks everyone.
[11:44] Alicia: thanks, appreciate the demo.
[11:47] Tom: thanks all.
[11:50] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker mislabels (Speaker 1), some internal runtime shorthand appears in UI; we will include a short glossary in the follow-up.
